rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is set beside the plea for no intercessors or close friend in 26:101.
rows.anchor: فما لنا من شافعين ولا صديق حميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No close friend asks after another on that Day because each is absorbed in his own affair, as in 80:37.
rows.anchor: لا يسأل الحميم عن حميمه في ذلك اليوم لأنه يذهب عن ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-maʿārij are places of ascent, rising by successive degrees; a lame person is so called because one leg is higher.
rows.anchor: اللغة: المعارج مواضع العروج وهو الصعود مرتبة بعد مرتبة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains al-muhl as the dregs of oil.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: المهل دردي الزيت.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation takes al-muhl as thick, turbid liquid flowing slowly; the word is linked to giving it time to flow.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو الجاري بغلظه وعكره على رفق من أمهله إمهالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿihn means fluffed wool.
rows.anchor: والعهن الصوف المنفوش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ḥamīm is a close relative, from the sense of nearness; the cited poetry uses it in this sense.
rows.anchor: والحميم القريب النسب إلى صاحبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ in biʿadhāb is governed by saʾala, understood as a caller invoking punishment.
rows.anchor: بعذاب الباء تتعلق بسأل لأن معناه دعا داع بعذاب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Alternatively, the bāʾ means ʿan, so the question is about the punishment.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن الباء بمعنى عن وتقديره عن عذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited poetry uses bi in the sense of ʿan: “ask about” a person's death and weapon.
rows.anchor: دع المعمر لا تسأل بمصرعه واسأل بمصقلة البكري ما فعلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in lil-kāfirīn means ʿalā and is governed by wāqiʿ: the punishment falls upon the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: بمعنى على ويتعلق بواقع أي واقع على الكافرين

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Alternatively, the lām attaches to an omitted phrase and describes the asker as one of the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: فيكون صفة لسائل تقديره سأل سائل كائن للكافرين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies the asker as al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who invoked punishment against himself after the claim quoted in 8:32.
rows.anchor: مستعجلا له وهو واقع بهم لا محالة عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the polytheists asked whom the punishment Muhammad mentioned would strike; the answer is the disbelievers, with none to repel it.
rows.anchor: فجاء جوابه بأنه { للكافرين ليس له دافع } عن الحسن

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi says the caller was the Prophet, praying for punishment upon the disbelievers; the bāʾ is extra for emphasis, as in 19:25.
rows.anchor: وذلك الداعي هو النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: On al-Jubbaʾi’s explanation, the bāʾ is emphatic and extra, as in the command cited from 19:25.
rows.anchor: وتكون الباء في بعذاب مزيدة على التوكيد كما في قوله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: On a reading with alif from sāla yasīlu, the phrase means that a stream of punishment flowed.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن معنى { سأل سائل } على قراءة من قرأ بالألف

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says Sāʾil is the name of a valley in Hell, named because punishment flows there.
rows.anchor: سائل اسم واد في جهنم سمي به لأنه يسيل بالعذاب عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid takes the thousand-year day as the angels’ ascent and descent between the lowest heaven and earth, five hundred years each way; humans would need that long to cross the same distance.
rows.anchor: هو لما بين السماء الدنيا والأرض في الصعود والنزول خمسمائة سنة في الصعود وخمسمائة سنة في النزول عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi, also followed here by Qatada and ʿIkrima, identifies the day as Resurrection, when worldly judgment would take fifty thousand years.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه يعني يوم القيامة وإنه يفعل فيه من الأمور ويقضي فيه من الأحكام

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abu Saʿid reports that the Prophet said this long Day will feel lighter to a believer than an obligatory prayer in worldly life.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو سعيد الخدري قال قيل يا رسول الله ما أطول هذا اليوم؟

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abu ʿAbd Allah says that if anyone but God handled the reckoning it would take fifty thousand years, while God completes it in an hour.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي عبد الله ع أنه قال: لو ولي الحساب غير الله

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abu ʿAbd Allah also says Paradise and Hell receive their inhabitants before half of that Day has passed.
rows.anchor: وعنه أيضا قال لا ينتصف ذلك اليوم حتى يقبل أهل الجنة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation measures the period from the angels’ first descent with commands and judgments until their final ascent at Resurrection; only God knows what has passed or remains.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه أن أول نزول الملائكة في الدنيا وأمره ونهيه وقضائه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj allows fī yawm to modify wāqiʿ: the punishment sought occurs on Resurrection Day.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: يجوز أن يكون قوله { في يوم } من صلة واقع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tells Muhammad to endure their denial with beautiful patience, without distress or complaint about what he suffers.
rows.anchor: { فاصبر } يا محمد على تكذيبهم إياك { صبرا جميلا } لا جزع فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers deem Resurrection distant because they reject it; God knows it is near, as everything that will come is near. The first “seeing” means supposing, the second knowing.
rows.anchor: فالرؤية الأولى بمعنى الظن والثانية بمعنى العلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas likens the sky to oil dregs.
rows.anchor: أي كدردي الزيت عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says the sky will resemble the turbid residue of tar.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كعكر القطران عن عطاء

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan compares the sky to silver after it has melted.
rows.anchor: وقيل: مثل الفضة إذا أذيبت عن الحسن

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim compares it to molten brass.
rows.anchor: وقيل: مثل الصفر المذاب عن أبي مسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mountains become colored wool, softening after their former hardness and separating after being gathered.
rows.anchor: { وتكون الجبال كالعهن } أي كالصوف المصبوغ

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil explains the mountains as fluffed wool.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كالصوف المنفوش عن مقاتل

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan describes the mountains as red wool and says they first crumble, then become fluffed wool, then scattered dust.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كالصوف الأحمر عن الحسن يعني أنها تلين بعد الشدة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says everyone is so occupied with himself that no close friend asks after another.
rows.anchor: لشغل كل إنسان بنفسه عن غيره عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says one close friend does not ask another to carry his sins because he has despaired of that help in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: لا يسأل حميم حميما أن يتحمل عنه من أوزاره ليأسه منه ذلك في الآخرة عن الحسن

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash defines a ḥamīm as someone specially loved, related by blood or not; al-ḥāmah means one’s close circle.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: الحميم من يخصه الرجل مودة وشفقة من قريب الرحم وبعيده

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says no one needs to ask, since people are recognizable by signs: disbelievers’ faces are black and eyes blue, while believers’ color is radiant and faces white.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه أنه لا يحتاج إلى سؤاله لأنه يكون لكل علامة يعرف بها

rows.speaker: حفص
rows.claim: Ḥafṣ reads nazzāʿatan in the accusative; the other readers use the nominative.
rows.anchor: قرأ حفص نزاعة بالنصب والباقون بالرفع

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir reads the trust in the singular, while the other readers use the plural.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير لأمانتهم بغير ألف بعد النون والباقون لأماناتهم بالجمع

rows.speaker: حفص ويعقوب وسهل
rows.claim: Ḥafṣ, Yaʿqub, and Sahl read “their testimonies” in the plural; the others use the singular.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حفص ويعقوب وسهل بشهاداتهم على الجمع والباقون بشهادتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All readers use the singular for “their prayer.”
rows.anchor: وكلهم قرؤوا على صلاتهم على التوحيد

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu ʿAli says the nominative nazzāʿatun works like a nominal predicate construction such as “this is Zayd departing.”
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: من قرأ { إنها لظى نزاعة للشوى } فرفع نزاعة جاز في رفعه

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: For the accusative, Abu ʿAli allows either a circumstantial accusative or an omitted verb; the circumstantial parse is weaker because there is no governor and Laẓā is definite.
rows.anchor: ومن نصب فعلى وجهين أحدهما: أن يكون حالا والآخر: أن يحمل على فعل

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu ʿAli says the circumstantial reading can work if Laẓā is understood through its newly salient quality of intense blazing.
rows.anchor: فإن جعلتها مع تعريفها قد صارت معروفة بشدة التلظي جاز أن تنصبه

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The accusative can alternatively depend on an omitted verb, with an understood phrase like “its eyes pull away the scalp.”
rows.anchor: وإن علقت نزاعة بفعل مضمر نحو أعينها نزاعة للشوى لم يمتنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular amānah is a collective verbal noun covering each individual’s trust; plural forms reflect the variety of trusts, and the same applies to testimony.
rows.anchor: لأنه مصدر يقع على جميع الجنس ويتناوله ومن جمع فلاختلاف الأمانات وكثرة ضروبها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laẓā is a name for Hell, derived from blazing.
rows.anchor: لظى اسم من أسماء جهنم مأخوذة من التوقد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nazzāʿah means repeatedly tearing away forcefully; shiwā is the skin of the head, singular shawāh.
rows.anchor: والنزاعة الكثيرة النزع وهو اقتلاع عن شدة ضم والاقتلاع أخذ بشدة اعتماد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shiwā is the skin of the head, and its singular is shawāh.
rows.anchor: والشوى جلدة الرأس واحدتها شواة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mawaddah can mean either wishing for something or loving it.
rows.anchor: اللغة: المودة مشتركة بين التمني وبين المحبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iftidāʾ means escaping harm by offering something in its place.
rows.anchor: والافتداء افتداء الضرر عن الشيء ببدل منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A faṣīlah is a branch group within a tribe, linked by a nearer ancestor beneath the broader ancestral line.
rows.anchor: والفصيلة الجماعة المنقطعة عن جملة القبيلة برجوعها إلى أبوة خاصة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar reads the opening annahu with fatḥ; he also uses fatḥ in the listed clauses through the jinn’s affirmations, with kasr in the other clauses except istiqāmū and al-masājid.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر { قل أوحي إلي أنه استمع } بفتح الألف

rows.speaker: الرواة عن أبي جعفر
rows.claim: His transmitters say clauses referred to revelation take fatḥ and the jinn’s own speech takes kasr, but this rule does not fit his reported reading; transmission may contain an error.
rows.anchor: قال الرواة عنه ما كان مردودا على الوحي فهو أنه بالفتح وما كان من قول الجن فهو بالكسر

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وأهل الكوفة غير أبي بكر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAmir and the Kufans except Abu Bakr read fatḥ from annahu taʿālā through wa-innā minnā al-muslimūn; the rest use kasr except the unanimously fatḥ-read clauses.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وأهل الكوفة غير أبي بكر بالفتح من قوله أنه تعالى إلى قوله

rows.speaker: نافع وعاصم برواية أبي بكر
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and ʿĀṣim in Abu Bakr’s transmission read wa-annahu lammā qāma with kasr; the other readers use fatḥ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وعاصم برواية أبي بكر وأنه لما قام بالكسر والباقون بالفتح

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: Yaʿqub, also reported from al-Jaḥdarī and al-Hasan, doubles the wāw in an lan taqūla and opens the specified vowels; the rest read it lightly.
rows.anchor: وقرأ يعقوب أن لن تقول بتشديد الواو وفتحها وفتح القاف

rows.speaker: جوية بن عابد
rows.claim: A rare reading attributed to Juwayya ibn ʿĀbid has qil aḥyi ilayya.
rows.anchor: وفي الشواذ قراءة جوية بن عابد قل أحي إلي

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu ʿAli parses an as the light form of anna, governed by revelation; law separates it from the verb as sin or lā can.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أن تكون أن المخففة من الثقيلة فيكون محمولا على الوحي كأنه أوحي إلي

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Alternatively, an before law is like an added lām before a conditional clause, since law functions like the conditional verb.
rows.anchor: والآخر: أن يكون أن قبل لو بمنزلة اللام في قوله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reported interpretation takes the path as the way of guidance.
rows.anchor: قد قيل فيه قولان أحدهما: لو استقاموا على طريقة الهدى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A second reported interpretation takes it as the way of disbelief.
rows.anchor: والآخر: لو استقاموا على طريقة الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guidance-path interpretation is supported by verses promising provision to those upholding revelation and blessings for believing, God-fearing towns.
rows.anchor: ولو أنهم أقاموا التوراة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The disbelief-path interpretation is supported by the possibility that people might otherwise become one community, prompting houses of silver for disbelievers.
rows.anchor: ويستدل على الآخر بقوله تعالى ولولا أن يكون الناس أمة واحدة

words: وَأَنَّ ٱلْمَسَٰجِدَ لِلَّهِ فَلَا تَدْعُوا۟ مَعَ ٱللَّهِ أَحَدًۭا
rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh says exegetes attach the mosques clause to “it was revealed to me”: it was revealed that the mosques belong to God.
rows.anchor: زعم سيبويه أن المفسرين حملوه على أوحي كأنه وأوحي إلي أن المساجد لله

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil instead supplies a causal “because”: because mosques belong to God, invoke no one alongside Him.
rows.anchor: ومذهب الخليل أنه على قوله ولأن المساجد لله فلا تدعوا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil compares this construction with “because your community is one” in 23:52 and “for this, worship Me” in 21:92, and with the construction in Sūrat Quraysh.
rows.anchor: كما أن قوله وأن هذه أمتكم

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh says reading wa-inna al-masājid with kasr would also be good.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه: ولو قرأ وإن المساجد بالكسر لكان جيدا

words: وَأَنَّهُۥ لَمَّا قَامَ عَبْدُ ٱللَّهَ يَدْعُوهُ
rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh connects wa-annahu lammā qāma to revelation; the clause can be cut off and begun independently, as with al-masājid.
rows.anchor: فإنه على { أوحي إلي } ويكون أن يقطع من قوله { أوحي }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥ, the clause may be attached to revelation, though another independent parse is possible.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ كل ذلك بالفتح فإنه للحمل على أوحي ويجوز أن يكون على غيره

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: After quoted speech and a conditional faʾ, the following clause can begin independently with an omitted introduction; Sibawayh applies this to examples including 72:23.
rows.anchor: وكذلك ما بعد فاء الجزاء لأن ما بعد فاء الجزاء موضع ابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the doubled reading, kadhiban is an accusative verbal noun without an omitted descriptive noun, because lan taqūla means “to lie.”
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ لن تقول فيكون قوله كذبا منصوبا على المصدر من غير حذف موصوف

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinni compares kadhiban governed by taqūla with “a flash” governed by “smiled,” where the verb means “flashed.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن جني ومن رأى أن ينتصب وميض البرق بنفس تبسمت لأنه في معنى أومضت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the light reading, kadhiban describes an omitted verbal noun, meaning “a false saying.”
rows.anchor: فإن كذبا وصف مصدر محذوف أي قولا كذبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the example from Joseph, kadhib means false or lying.
rows.anchor: وجاءوا على قميصه بدم كذب [يوسف: 18] أي كاذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rare form aḥyi comes from waḥaytu ilayhi, meaning awḥaytu; initial wāw becomes hamza after obligatory ḍamma, as in uqit for wuqqit.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ أحي فهو من وحيت إليه بمعنى أوحيت وأصله وحي

rows.speaker: العجاج
rows.claim: Al-ʿAjjāj’s verse uses waḥā as a witness for the root form.
rows.anchor: قال العجاج: وحى لها القرار فاستقرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jadd originally means cutting; related senses include greatness by surpassing others, grandfather by elevated ancestry, fortune by rank, the opposite of joking, and “new” as recently cut.
rows.anchor: الجد أصله القطع ومنه الجد العظمة لانقطاع كل عظمة عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahq means the catching up of sin; its root sense is overtaking, as in a youth reaching the condition of a man.
rows.anchor: والرهق لحاق الإثم وأصله اللحوق ومنه راهق الغلام إذا لحق حال الرجال

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā’s verse uses rahq for committing or being tainted by sin.
rows.anchor: قال الأعشى: لا شيء ينفعني من دون رؤيتها هل يشتفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥarasan is an accusative of specification; alternatively it is the plural ḥarasī, like ʿarab from ʿarabī.
rows.anchor: حرسا منصوب على التمييز وهو جمع حارس ويجوز أن يكون جمع حرسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shadīdan is masculine by agreement with the word’s grammatical form; alternatively it is relational, meaning “possessing severity.”
rows.anchor: وشديدا مذكر محمول على اللفظ ويمكن أن يكون على النسبة أي ذات شدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maqāʿid is accusative as a locative adverb.
rows.anchor: ومقاعد نصب لأنه ظرف مكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a-sharrun urīda, a-sharr is the subject and urīda its predicate; an indefinite may begin a clause after an interrogative hamza because it conveys generality like negation.
rows.anchor: أشر أريد مبتدأ وخبر وإنما جاز أن تكون النكرة مبتدأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God commands Muhammad to tell his people what they did not know; the passive “it was revealed” magnifies the revelation, which God sent through an angel.
rows.anchor: إنما ذكره على لفظ ما لم يسم فاعله تفخيما وتعظيما والله سبحانه أوحى إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinn are light-bodied beings in a distinctive form, unlike humans made of clay and angels made of light; jinn are made of fire.
rows.anchor: وهم جيل رقاق الأجسام خفيفة على صورة مخصوصة بخلاف صورة الإنسان والملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They said” means that some of the jinn spoke to the others.
rows.anchor: فقالوا } أي قالت الجن بعضها لبعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is wondrous because its distinctive composition exceeds ordinary speech, its cause is hidden, and it differs from human speech in meaning, eloquence, and form; none can match it.
rows.anchor: فلما كان القرآن قد خرج بتأليفه المخصوص عن العادة في الكلام وخفي سببه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its wonder also lies in recounting past and future events through an unlettered man among an unlettered people.
rows.anchor: وقد تضمن أخبار الأولين والآخرين وما كان وما يكون أجراه الله على يد رجل أمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an points to and calls toward guidance; rushd is the opposite of error.
rows.anchor: أي يدل على الهدى ويدعو إليه والرشد ضد الضلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn believe the Qur’an is from God, abandon shirk, and dedicate worship to Him, beginning by accepting truth and affirming divine unity.
rows.anchor: بل نخلص العبادة لله تعالى والمعنى أنا قد بدأنا بأنفسنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage shows Muhammad was sent to jinn and humans, and that jinn are rational, accountable, know Arabic, recognize miracles, and invited their people to Islam and the Qur’an’s inimitability.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا دلالة على أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم كان مبعوثا إلى الجن والإنس وعلى أن الجن عقلاء مخاطبون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi transmits from Ibn ʿAbbas through Saʿid ibn Jubayr that the Prophet neither recited to nor saw the jinn: after being barred from heavenly news, a group heard his dawn recitation at Nakhlah near ʿUkāẓ and returned to their people. Bukhari and Muslim also report it in their Ṣaḥīḥs.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس قال: ما قرأ رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم على الجن

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view understands istiqāmah as remaining on the path of guidance, supported by promises of provision and blessings for those who uphold revelation and believe.
rows.anchor: ولو أنهم أقاموا التوراة [المائدة: 66] إلى قوله لأكلوا من فوقهم

rows.speaker: الفراء والربيع والكلبي والثمالي وأبو مسلم وابن مجلز
rows.claim: Another view takes the path as disbelief: if all disbelieved, God would give abundant wealth to intensify the trial.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه لو استقاموا على طريقة الكفر فكانوا كفارا كلهم لأعطيناهم مالا كثيرا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ explains “to test them through it” as a heavy trial in worship, requiring restraint from desires; reward follows the hardship of patience.
rows.anchor: عن الفراء وهو قول الربيع والكلبي والثمالي وأبي مسلم وابن مجلز

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar says that wherever there is water there is wealth, and wherever there is wealth there is temptation.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عمر بن الخطاب أنه قال في هذه الآية أينما كان الماء كان المال

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب وقتادة ومقاتل والحسن
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, Qatada, Muqatil, and al-Hasan say the trial is to test how people give thanks for blessings.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه لنختبرهم كيف يكون شكرهم للنعم عن سعيد بن المسيب وقتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers istiqāmah in religion and faith, since that is the usual sense and this context gently summons people to faith and obedience.
rows.anchor: والأولى أن تكون الاستقامة على الطريقة محمولة على الاستقامة في الدين والإيمان

rows.speaker: أبو بصير
rows.claim: In a report from the Ahl al-Bayt commentary, Abu Baṣīr asks Abu Jaʿfar about 41:30; Abu Jaʿfar says the verse means the belief held by his interlocutors.
rows.anchor: وفي تفسير أهل البيت ع عن أبي بصير قال قلت لأبي جعفر ع قول الله

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abu ʿAbd Allah interprets abundant water as abundant knowledge learned from the Imams.
rows.anchor: وعن بريد العجلي عن أبي عبد الله ع قال: معناه لأفدناهم علما كثيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning from the Lord’s remembrance means turning away from reflection leading to knowledge of God, unity, and sincere worship.
rows.anchor: ومن يعدل عن الفكر فيما يؤديه إلى معرفة الله وتوحيده والإخلاص في عبادته

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation takes the Lord’s remembrance as gratitude to God and obedience to Him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عن شكر الله وطاعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “make him enter” echoes the preceding mention of a path; ṣaʿad means a difficult, severe, ascending punishment.
rows.anchor: وإنما قال يسلكه لأنه تقدم ذكر الطريقة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation reads ṣaʿad as “possessing hardship.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه عذابا ذا صعد أي ذا مشقة

words: وَأَنَّ ٱلْمَسَٰجِدَ لِلَّهِ فَلَا تَدْعُوا۟ مَعَ ٱللَّهِ أَحَدًۭا
rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil’s construction means: because mosques belong to God, invoke no one besides Him in them.
rows.anchor: تقديره ولأن المسجد لله فلا تدعوا مع الله أحدا سوى الله عن الخليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command forbids invoking anyone alongside God in places built for prayer, as Christians do in churches and polytheists do at the Kaʿba.
rows.anchor: لا تذكروا مع الله في المواضع التي بنيت للعبادة والصلاة أحدا على وجه الإشراك

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says it is Sunnah on entering mosques to declare that there is no god but God and that one invokes no one alongside Him.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: من السنة عند دخول المساجد أن يقال لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير والزجاج والفراء
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Zajjaj, and al-Farraʾ take “mosques” as the seven body parts used in prostration, which belong to God and should prostrate to no one else.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المساجد مواضع السجود من الإنسان وهي الجبهة والكفان

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر بن علي بن موسى الرضا
rows.claim: When al-Muʿtaṣim asked, Abu Jaʿfar ibn ʿAli ibn Musa al-Riḍā answered that the mosques are the seven body parts on which one prostrates.
rows.anchor: وروي أن المعتصم سأل أبا جعفر بن علي بن موسى الرضا ع عن قوله

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Another view from al-Hasan takes the mosques as all regions of the earth, which God made a place of prayer for Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن المراد بالمساجد البقاع كلها وذلك لأن الأرض كلها جعلت

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr reports that the jinn asked how they could reach the mosque and pray with the Prophet from far away, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: قالت الجن للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: كيف لنا أن نأتي المسجد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan also interprets mosques as the prayers themselves: worship should be devoted to God alone, with no share given to another.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الحسن أيضا أن المساجد الصلوات وهي لله والمراد أخلصوا لله العبادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The servant of God” refers to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: يريد به محمدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad was calling people with “There is no god but God,” inviting them to it, and reciting the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: بقول لا إله إلا الله ويدعو إليه ويقرأ القرآن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say the jinn nearly piled on one another around Muhammad, eager to hear the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس والضحاك

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says the jinn told their people that the Prophet’s companions crowded around him to hear the Qur’an, each wanting to be closest.
rows.anchor: فيتلبد بعضهم على بعض عن سعيد بن جبير.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view treats the clause as part of what God revealed about the jinn’s eagerness to listen.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو من جملة ما أوحى الله إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: قتادة والحسن
rows.claim: Qatada and al-Hasan say Quraysh crowded around Muhammad to overwhelm him and stop his call to monotheism, but God gave him victory.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة والحسن وعلى هذا فيكون ابتداء كلام

words: قُلْ إِنَّمَآ أَدْعُوا۟ رَبِّى وَلَآ أُشْرِكُ بِهِۦٓ أَحَدًۭا
rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the opponents told Muhammad to abandon his unprecedented, momentous message; he was commanded to answer that he invokes only his Lord.
rows.anchor: وذلك أنهم قالوا للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إنك جئت بأمر عظيم لم يسمع مثله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reply rejects associating anyone with God and supports the view that the preceding crowd is Quraysh pressing Muhammad to stop preaching.
rows.anchor: وهذا يعضد قول الحسن وقتادة لأنه كالذم لهم على ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report recounts that Muhammad recited 40:1–3 in the mosque while al-Walid ibn al-Mughira listened, repeated the passage when he noticed, and al-Walid praised its sweetness and power.
rows.anchor: قام إلى المسجد والوليد بن المغيرة قريب منه يسمع قراءته فلما فطن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أبو جهل
rows.claim: Quraysh feared al-Walid would convert and others follow; Abu Jahl prompted him to dismiss Muhammad’s speech, and al-Walid called it sorcery because it divides families.
rows.anchor: فقالت قريش صبأ والله الوليد والله لتصبأن قريش كلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tells Muhammad to leave the described unbeliever to Him, for God will punish him; the phrase is an idiom meaning “leave me and him.”
rows.anchor: أي دعني وإياه فإني كاف له في عقابه كما يقول القائل دعني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If waḥīdan describes the created man, it means he was created alone in his mother’s womb, without wealth or children; the man is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.
rows.anchor: وإن حملته على صفة المخلوق فمعناه دعني ومن خلقته في بطن أمه واحد

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil glosses the command as “leave him between Me and him,” since God will destroy him alone.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: معناه خل بيني وبينه فأنا أفرد بهلكته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says al-Walid was known as “the Unique One” among his people.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: كان الوليد يسمى الوحيد في قومه

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: A report from al-ʿAyyashi says Abu Jaʿfar explained al-waḥīd as a child of unknown paternity; boasting “son of the unique one” would therefore be shameful.
rows.anchor: أن الوحيد ولد الزنا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbas describes wealth from Mecca to Ṭāʾif: herds, fine horses and livestock, enduring revenues, enslaved people, and abundant cash.
rows.anchor: النعم المرحلة والمستغلات التي لا تنقطع غلتها والجواري والعبيد والعين الكثيرة عن عطاء عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the wealth’s yield never stopped from year to year; al-Walid had a productive Taʾif orchard, ten sons, and one hundred thousand dinars.
rows.anchor: وكان له بستان بالطائف لا ينقطع خيره في شتاء ولا صيف وعشرة بنين ومائة ألف دينار عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada estimates al-Walid’s wealth at six thousand dinars.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ستة آلاف دينار عن قتادة

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyan estimates al-Walid’s wealth at four thousand dinars.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أربعة آلاف دينار عن سفيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His sons were present with him in Mecca and did not travel for commerce because their wealth made it unnecessary.
rows.anchor: حضورا معه بمكة لا يغيبون عنه لغناهم عن ركوب السفر للتجارة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says al-Walid had thirteen sons.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير: كانوا ثلاثة عشر

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says al-Walid had seven sons and names them; Khalid, Hisham, and ʿUmārah became Muslim.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: كانوا سبعة الوليد وخالد وعمارة وهشام والعاص وقيس وعبد شمس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The report says al-Walid’s wealth and children continued to decline after this passage until his death.
rows.anchor: قالوا فما زال الوليد بعد هذه الآية في نقصان من ماله وولده حتى هلك
